and it carries through a promise President Trump made in his executive order for AI security early last month.
Security experts are saying the program – which the Trump Administration is calling “
” – does address such important issues as the duplication of effort by multiple security vendors in scanning for software bugs
. However, they add that finding the vulnerabilities isn’t the key problem. Security teams are swimming in known security flaws.

Cobalt CTO Gunter Ollmann said coordination of vulnerability data across industries and government is “the right instinct” given the time wasted by analysts duplicating scanning.

That said, “finding vulnerabilities has not been the hard part for a while now,” Ollmann said. “Prioritizing them against real exploitability and getting remediation into the hands of the right owner is where most programs break down, and that’s a coordination and workflow problem, not something AI alone resolves.”

“Routing better-prioritized guidance to defenders who already can’t keep pace with their backlog doesn’t change throughput on its own,” said Justin Beals, founder and CEO of Strike Graph. “The programs that move the needle pair discovery with a measurement and accountability model downstream. If Gold Eagle has that second half, it will matter. The [White House press] release only describes the first.”

The White House sees Gold Eagle as a way to track down – and mitigate – critical vulnerabilities found by frontier AI models before they can be exploited by threat groups, which usually are using the same AI capabilities.
In their release, administration officials said

will “leverage frontier AI capabilities to continue advancing faster than adversaries, reduce duplicative scanning efforts, and deliver prioritized and actionable threat and remediation information to defenders across the Federal government and the private sector,” adding that it’s a “force multiplier, enabling government and industry to collectively identify risks, prioritize action, and strengthen the resilience of the systems that power our economy, national security, and daily life.

”Work Already is Underway “Through this strategic partnership, we will expand existing security measures to safeguard software and networks in the 21st century and continue to promote advancements in artificial intelligence,” Markwayne Mullin, newly appointed Department of Homeland Security (DHS) secretary, said in a statement. The program already has begun taking in and prioritizing identified vulnerabilities and coordinate the verification of the scans, according to the administration. Developing Gold Eagle involved not only the White House and federal offices like Treasury, DHS, CISA, and the Defense Department, but also cybersecurity and open source software companies. Running on VINCE Gold Eagle will operate atop the Vulnerability Information and Coordination Environment (VINCE), which the agencies will run with Carnegie Mellon University’s Software Engineering Institute. Anyone reporting a bug for triage and mitigation will do so through VINCE. The initiative comes after Anthropic’s introduction in April of Mythos and its Project Glasswing cybersecurity initiative. Mythos showed not only significant capabilities in detecting security flaws but also the ability to rapidly develop exploits. Anthropic – like OpenAI with its frontier models – initially limited access to Mythos but has since expanded who can use it. Security pros applauded the coordination between multiple government agencies and the private sector, as well as the decision to base it on VINCE, given what Jacob Krell, senior director of secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, called “the Software Engineering Institute’s decades of experience with coordinated vulnerability disclosure.” ‘Directionally the Right Model’ Donald McFarlane, advisory board member for Xcape, said such public-private partnerships in cybersecurity are “directionally the right model” and that “execution will determine whether it becomes transformative or merely another information-sharing program.” “Frontier AI is already changing the scale and speed of vulnerability discovery while accelerating offensive cyber operations,” McFarlane said. “The real challenges are shifting toward coordination, prioritization, elimination of duplicate effort, and maintaining a defensive advantage when adversaries have access to many of the same capabilities.”
